catalog_quote: § 5. Quantitative distinctions between vowels in modern Ossetic do not have phonemic significance. But formerly these distinctions were very essential and as the result of this past status, the modern vowels may be divided into two groups: strong: а е и о у; weak: æ ы. The former group can be traced back, as a rule, to the old long vowels or diphthongs; the latter, to the old short vowels. Even today the strong vowels remain somewhat longer. ... § 30. In Ossetic, the stress is expiratory (intensive). In the flow of speech, it is not the stress of the individual word, as in Russian, which is crucial, but rather the phrase stress. Word groups that are syntactically connected in some way, are joined together by a single stress. ... § 31. The occurrence of stress, both in separate words and in accentual groups, is subject to the following regularities: .1 The stress falls only on the first …
sweep_summary: Modern Ossetic is in the catalog as 'weight' (Abaev 1964 §5, §§30-31: stress on the first syllable if its vowel is strong, otherwise on the second). The sweep had two Glottolog items, which are one work: Cheung 1999, 'Some remarks on the history of the Ossetic accent', in van den Berg (ed.), Studies in Caucasian linguistics (Leiden: CNWS), 286-292 — the second item attributes it to the volume's editor and is a Glottolog duplicate. HAL holds the record (author's lab; one-line abstract, no file); HathiTrust has the volume search-only; Google Books, HathiTrust and the Leiden repository were blocked/unreachable from our machine; OpenAlex/S2/CORE/archive.org gave nothing. The paper itself was not read (medium priority; diachronic, 7 pages; its fuller form is Cheung 2002:121ff, print/paywalled). While hunting it I found and read an open first-hand statement by the same author (Cheung 2008/2018, Nartamongæ XIII: 103-104, n.1 and n.13): historical (pre-)Ossetic had initial stress; the modern 'rhythmic-like' accent 'determined by the quantity/quality of the vowels' is secondary — this confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding and does not supersede Abaev 1964. Two paywalled reviews of the 1999 volume (Vajda, Language 77(2) 2001; Friedman, Studies in Language 25(2) 2001) and Schmitt's Kratylos 49 (2004) review of Cheung 2002 are low-priority leads. All fetched sources

new_statements.quote: An important difference in opinion between us is the treatment of the Ossetic (historical) accent, for which I argued initial stress (Cheung 2002:121 ff.), whereas Kim called for a Sogdian-like stress based on heavy and light stems. [...] The "rhythmic-like" accent, being determined by the quantity/quality of the vowels, which we see in modern Ossetic cannot be but of secondary origin.
new_statements.citation: Cheung, Johnny. 2018 [2008]. The Ossetic case system revisited. Nartamongæ XIII(1-2): 87-105 (reprint of the 2008 Kortlandt Festschrift paper, Rodopi, 87-105).
new_statements.locator: note 1, pp. 103-104 (reprint pagination); cf. note 13, p. 104
new_statements.reading: The author of the sweep's only target paper states first-hand that modern Ossetic word accent is 'rhythmic-like' and 'determined by the quantity/quality of the vowels' (the strong/weak vowel distinction), i.e. the catalog's 'weight' coding, and that this is a secondary development from an older initial-stress system (his 1999 paper and 2002 book, pp. 121ff., argue the diachronic point). It confirms the catalog's synchronic coding without adding detail on the placement rule; it is a footnote in a paper on case morphology, so it does not displace Abaev 1964 as the deciding source.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No correction to the bearing. Locator fix only: note 1 runs pp. 103-104 (PDF pp. 17-18, printed page numbers visible) as stated, but note 13 is on the unnumbered final page = p. 105 (PDF p. 19), not p. 104. The footnote corroborates the catalog's 'weight' (strong/weak-vowel) coding as a specialist aside; it gives no placement rule and does not displace Abaev 1964 §§5, 30-31, 35.

audit.deciding_source_year: 1964 (English translation, IJAL 30(4) pt.2, 133 pp.; Russian original Grammaticheskij ocherk osetinskogo jazyka, 1959, reprinted in Osetinsko-russkij slovar' 2nd ed. 1962 per the Iranica bibliography)
audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation (Abaev 1964 secs 5, 30, 31, plus sec.35) is verbatim in the held archive.org PDF and its text extracts at the stated printed pages 4-5, 10-11 and 12; a second reader pass on 2026-09-12 had already re-read the page images and 20 stress-marked forms. (2) The classification rests on a 1964 English translation of Abaev's grammatical sketch: a short but primary and authoritative description, and the source every database entry (StressTyp2, Hayes, Hyman) derives from. Glottolog's 'grammar' list is mostly syntax papers; the genuinely fuller descriptions are the Russian reference grammars (Akhvlediani ed. 1963; Bagaev 1965) and the instrumental work of Sokolova 1953 and Dzakhova 2010, all open and fetched sources now to ( record there). Each restates the same system: stress confined to syllables 1-2 of the word/accentual

[...] The "rhythmic-like" accent, being determined by the quantity/quality of the vowels, which we see in modern Ossetic cannot be but of secondary origin. [n.13:] ... in line with my arguments of initial stress in (pre-)Oss. and again suggests the secondary character of voweldependent accent in modern Oss.
sources.note: First-hand statement by the author of item 1: modern Ossetic has a 'rhythmic-like', vowel-dependent accent 'determined by the quantity/quality of the vowels' (i.e. the strong/weak vowel conditioning the catalog codes as 'weight'); historically (pre-Ossetic) Cheung argues for initial stress, against Kim 2003's Sogdian-style heavy/light-stem rule. The paper itself is about case morphology; the accent statements are in the notes.

sources.quote: 'The accent is a weak expiratory stress. Word accent is subordinate to phrase accent. The flow of speech is divided into prosodic groups, where a single syllable carries the main accent; a secondary accent may fall on other syllables in the group. As a rule, the first syllable of the group is stressed if the vowel is long; if it is short, the second syllable is stressed. In Iron, where an initial i is lost, the first syllable of the group is stressed, although the vowel is short. This happens when the definite article, still preserved in Digor, has been elided ... sources.citation: Dzakhova, V. T. 2010. Ob osetinskom udarenii [On Ossetic stress]. Vestnik RGGU. Serija Literaturovedenie. Jazykoznanie. Kul'turologija, 2010, pp. 9-23 (open, CyberLeninka).
sources.quote: p.10 summarises Abaev, Isaev, Grammatika 1963 and Bagaev: '1. Stress in Ossetic words can fall only on the first or second syllable; beyond the second only in Russian loans. 2. If the first syllable has a strong vowel (a, e, i, o, u) and the second a weak one (y, ae), stress falls on the first syllable [exceptions listed] ... if the first is weak and the second strong, stress falls on the second. 3. If both first syllables are strong, stress most often falls on the first ... 4. weak vowels in both first syllables -> as a rule the second'. p.11: hence Ossetic stress is 'bound'; an audio diction
sources.locator: p.10 (place of stress), p.11, p.15 Table 1, p.17, p.21, p.23 (conclusion + appendix)

sources.quote: sec.104: Ossetic stress expiratory, 'not particularly intensive, so many often do not distinguish which syllable is stressed'; Iron stress more intensive than Digor. sec.106: '1. Stress falls either on the first or on the second syllable from the beginning ... Beyond the second syllable stress can occur only in words borrowed from Russian'; '2. The place of stress on the first or second syllable depends basically on the quality of the vowels': (a) strong V1 + weak V2 -> syll 1 (exceptions abyraeg, xalyvvae, Iryston, iron, izaer ... mostly loans); (b) weak V1 + strong V2 -> syll 2; (v) weak+wea
sources.note: Fullest native reference treatment of Iron stress (secs 104-108, pp.56-62ff) with explicit exception lists, prefix/suffix behaviour, proper-name rule and accentual-complex rules; our record rests on Abaev's 2-page sketch statement. fetched sources; confirms/refines.

sources.quote: In the present work a comprehensive account of some important developments which took place in the phonology of that language is given. The developments comprise apocope (loss of final vowel), syncope (loss of medial vowel), aphaeresis (loss of initial vowel), i-epenthesis (insertion of *i) and accompanying palatalization, and finally, the fate of *u. Also the role of the accent in these cases is addressed. (HAL abstract)
sources.note: Not read. Per the author's own later summary it argues for initial stress in (pre-)Ossetic (pp. 121ff.) and treats the modern vowel-dependent accent as secondary; the fullest version of the argument sketched in item 1. Print/paywalled; no open copy located (Leiden repository unreachable from our machine).
